eras.title: Predynastic Egypt
eras.text: Communities along the Nile develop into the rival kingdoms of Upper and Lower Egypt, which King Narmer unites around 3150 BC.

eras.title: The Old Kingdom
eras.text: Unified Egypt is ruled by god-kings from Memphis. The pyramids are built at Giza, and hieroglyphic writing and a powerful bureaucracy develop.

eras.title: Middle Kingdom and the Hyksos
eras.text: After a period of collapse, the Middle Kingdom reunites Egypt and conquers Nubia; later the Hyksos from the Levant rule the north.

eras.title: The New Kingdom empire
eras.text: Egypt's imperial age: pharaohs such as Thutmose III, Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II rule from Nubia to Syria and are buried in the Valley of the Kings.

eras.title: Late Period
eras.text: Egypt is divided and ruled in turn by Libyans, the Kingdom of Kush, Assyrians and Persians, with brief native revivals.

eras.title: Greek and Roman Egypt
eras.text: Alexander's general Ptolemy founds a dynasty ruling from Alexandria; after Cleopatra, Egypt becomes Rome's granary and later a Christian (Coptic) land.

eras.title: Islamic Egypt
eras.text: Arab armies conquer Egypt. Under the Fatimids and then the Mamluks, Cairo becomes one of the greatest cities of the Islamic world.

eras.title: Ottoman Egypt and Muhammad Ali
eras.text: The Ottomans rule Egypt; after Napoleon's invasion (1798) Muhammad Ali begins modernising the country. The Suez Canal opens in 1869.

eras.title: British occupation to independence
eras.text: Britain occupies Egypt (1882). Formal independence comes in 1922; Nasser's revolution (1952) and the Suez Crisis (1956) end British influence. Egypt remains the Arab world's most populous country.

eras.title: The slave-soldier sultans
eras.text: Mamluks — slave soldiers of Turkic and Circassian origin — seize power in Egypt, defeat the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260) and expel the last Crusaders (1291). The Ottomans conquer the sultanate in 1517.

eras.title: The Shia caliphate of Cairo
eras.text: An Ismaili Shia dynasty rises in North Africa, conquers Egypt (969) and founds Cairo and al-Azhar. Its Red Sea trade links India to the Mediterranean; Saladin ends the dynasty in 1171.

eras.title: The golden age of Baghdad
eras.text: The Abbasids rule from their new round city of Baghdad. Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun it is the world's intellectual capital: Greek, Persian and Indian works are translated, and scholars like al-Khwarizmi (algebra) flourish.

eras.title: Caliphs without power
eras.text: Real power passes to Persian Buyids and then Seljuk Turks, while the caliph remains a religious figurehead. The Mongols sack Baghdad and kill the last Abbasid caliph in 1258.

eras.title: The first Islamic dynasty
eras.text: Ruling from Damascus, the Umayyads expand the caliphate from the Iberian Peninsula to Central Asia, build the Dome of the Rock, and make Arabic the language of government.

sources.title: Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula

eras.title: Al-Andalus
eras.text: A refugee Umayyad prince founds an emirate in Spain; Abd al-Rahman III proclaims a caliphate (929). Córdoba, with its Great Mosque and libraries, is Western Europe's largest city. It breaks up into taifa kingdoms in 1031.

eras.title: Berber reformers
eras.text: A puritanical Berber movement rules Morocco and al-Andalus from Marrakesh. The philosophers Averroes and Maimonides live under its rule. Defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) begins its collapse.

eras.title: The Great Seljuks
eras.text: Oghuz Turks conquer Iran and Iraq, take Baghdad (1055) as protectors of the Abbasid caliph, and defeat Byzantium at Manzikert (1071), opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

eras.title: Sultanate of Rum
eras.text: A branch of the Seljuks rules central Anatolia from Konya as the Sultanate of Rum. After the Mongols defeat it, Anatolia breaks up into Turkish beyliks, one of which becomes the Ottoman state.

eras.title: Mongol Persia
eras.text: Hülegü, grandson of Genghis Khan, founds a Mongol state in Iran and Iraq after sacking Baghdad. The Ilkhans convert to Islam (1295) and preside over a Persian cultural revival.

eras.title: Timur's conquests
eras.text: Timur, also known as Tamerlane, founds the Timurid Empire in 1370 and conquers Greater Iran, much of Central Asia and parts of India and Anatolia, ruling from Samarkand until his death in 1405.

eras.title: The Timurid Renaissance
eras.text: His successors rule Iran and Central Asia from Herat and Samarkand; Ulugh Beg builds an observatory and Persian miniature painting peaks.

eras.title: The Achaemenid Persian Empire
eras.text: Cyrus the Great and Darius I build the largest empire the world had yet seen, from Egypt and Greece's edge to the Indus, linked by the Royal Road. Alexander the Great conquers it.

eras.title: Parthia
eras.text: The Parthian Arsacids rule Iran and Mesopotamia and halt Roman expansion to the east, controlling trade between Rome and China.

eras.title: The Sasanian Empire
eras.text: A Zoroastrian Persian empire, Rome's great rival for four centuries. Exhausted by war with the Byzantine Empire, it falls to the Arab conquests.

eras.title: Islamic Persia
eras.text: Iran becomes Muslim but keeps its language; Persian becomes the high culture of the eastern Islamic world. It is ruled by Arabs, Persian dynasties, Turks, Mongols and Timurids.

eras.title: The Safavids
eras.text: Shah Ismail makes Shia Islam the state religion. Shah Abbas the Great rebuilds Isfahan as one of the world's most beautiful cities and trades silk with Europe.

eras.title: Afsharids and Qajars
eras.text: Nader Shah sacks Delhi (1739). The Qajar dynasty loses territory to Russia and becomes a pawn in the 'Great Game' between Russia and Britain.

eras.title: Pahlavis and the Islamic Republic
eras.text: Reza Shah modernises by force; oil becomes central. The 1979 revolution creates an Islamic Republic under Ayatollah Khomeini.

eras.title: Old and Middle Assyria
eras.text: A trading city-state on the Tigris becomes a regional power.

eras.title: The Neo-Assyrian Empire
eras.text: Assyria's ruthless army conquers Mesopotamia, the Levant and Egypt. Its kings build palaces at Nineveh decorated with reliefs, and Ashurbanipal collects a great library. Babylon and the Medes destroy it in 612 BC.

eras.title: Old Babylon
eras.text: Hammurabi makes Babylon the capital of Mesopotamia and issues his famous law code.

eras.title: Kassite and Assyrian eras
eras.text: Babylon is ruled by the Kassites, then often by Assyria, but remains the region's cultural centre.

eras.title: Neo-Babylonian Empire
eras.text: Nebuchadnezzar II builds the Ishtar Gate and (perhaps) the Hanging Gardens and destroys Jerusalem. Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon in 539 BC.

eras.title: The Hittite Empire
eras.text: From Hattusa in central Anatolia, the Hittites rule a great empire, fight Egypt at Kadesh and sign the earliest known peace treaty. They collapse in the Bronze Age collapse.

eras.title: Elam
eras.text: An ancient civilisation in south-west Iran, with its capital at Susa, Elam is a long-time rival and trading partner of the Mesopotamian states until absorbed by Persia.

eras.title: Minoan Crete
eras.text: A Bronze Age civilisation of palaces (Knossos, Phaistos), frescoes and sea trade, writing in Linear A. After the Thera eruption it is taken over by Mycenaean Greeks.

eras.title: Phoenician trading empire
eras.text: Carthage grows into the leading power of the western Mediterranean, with colonies in Spain, Sardinia and Sicily.

eras.title: The Punic Wars
eras.text: Three wars with Rome: Carthage loses Sicily, then Hannibal invades Italy but is defeated at Zama (202 BC). Rome destroys the city in 146 BC.

eras.title: The Ptolemies
eras.text: A Greek dynasty rules Egypt from Alexandria, home to the Great Library and Lighthouse. The last ruler, Cleopatra VII, allies with Caesar and Mark Antony before Rome annexes Egypt.

eras.title: The Seleucids
eras.text: Alexander's general Seleucus inherits the eastern empire from Syria to Afghanistan. It shrinks under pressure from Parthia and Rome, which annexes Syria in 63 BC.

eras.title: Napata and the Black Pharaohs
eras.text: The Nubian kingdom of Kush builds pyramids at Napata and conquers Egypt, ruling it as the 25th Dynasty.

eras.title: Meroë
eras.text: The capital moves south to Meroë, a centre of iron-working with its own script and pyramids. Aksum eclipses it in the 4th century.

eras.title: Aksum
eras.text: A trading empire in Ethiopia and Eritrea that controls Red Sea commerce between Rome and India, mints its own coins, raises giant stone stelae and converts to Christianity in the 4th century.

eras.title: The Zagwe dynasty
eras.text: King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty commissions churches carved from the rock as a new Jerusalem.

eras.title: The Solomonic empire
eras.text: A dynasty claiming descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba rules Christian Ethiopia. It fights the Adal Sultanate and, with Portuguese help, survives the invasion of Imam Ahmad (1529–1543).

eras.title: Gondar and the Era of Princes
eras.text: Emperors build castles at Gondar; later regional lords rule while emperors are figureheads.

eras.title: Modern Ethiopia
eras.text: Tewodros and Menelik II reunite and expand Ethiopia, which defeats Italy at Adwa (1896) and stays independent through the Scramble for Africa. Italy occupies it from 1936 to 1941. Haile Selassie rules until 1974.

eras.title: The empire of gold
eras.text: Sundiata Keita founds the Mali Empire. Under Mansa Musa (1312–37), whose pilgrimage to Mecca dazzled Cairo, it is one of the richest states in the world, controlling West Africa's gold fields and the scholarly city of Timbuktu.

eras.title: Decline
eras.text: Succession struggles and the rise of Songhai shrink Mali to its Mande heartland.

eras.title: Songhai
eras.text: Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad build the largest empire in West African history along the Niger, with Timbuktu and Djenné as centres of trade and Islamic learning. A Moroccan army with firearms destroys it in 1591.

eras.title: The land of gold
eras.text: Ghana (Wagadu), in today's Mauritania and Mali, grows rich by taxing the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt. Arab writers call it the land of gold.

eras.title: The stone city
eras.text: Shona kings build the great stone enclosures of Great Zimbabwe and grow rich on gold traded to the Swahili coast.

eras.title: Around Lake Chad
eras.text: One of Africa's longest-lasting states, ruled by the Sayfawa dynasty around Lake Chad, trading horses, slaves and ivory across the Sahara and adopting Islam in the 11th century.

eras.title: Kingdom of Benin
eras.text: A powerful kingdom in today's southern Nigeria (not modern Benin), famed for its walled capital and brass plaques. It trades with the Portuguese from the 1480s, until the British sack Benin City in 1897.

eras.title: Kingdom of Kongo
eras.text: A centralised kingdom near the Congo River's mouth; its king converts to Christianity after the Portuguese arrive (1483) and corresponds with the pope, but the Atlantic slave trade tears it apart.

eras.title: Under Portuguese overlordship
eras.text: From 1862 the Kingdom of Kongo is intermittently a vassal state of Portugal. After suppressing a Kongo revolt in 1914, Portugal abolishes the monarchy, and the kingdom's remaining lands are absorbed into Portuguese Angola.

eras.title: The Hafsids of Tunis
eras.text: A Berber dynasty rules Tunisia and eastern Algeria from Tunis, until the Ottomans take Tunis in the 16th century.

eras.title: Berber and Arab dynasties
eras.text: Idrisids, Almoravids, Almohads, Marinids and Wattasids rule Morocco, often also al-Andalus, from cities like Fez and Marrakesh.

eras.title: Saadis and Alaouites
eras.text: Sharifian dynasties keep Morocco independent of the Ottomans; the Saadis destroy the Songhai Empire (1591).

eras.title: Protectorate and independence
eras.text: France and Spain divide Morocco into protectorates; it regains independence in 1956.

eras.title: The Turkish Republic
eras.text: Atatürk builds a secular nation-state from the Ottoman ruins: the Latin alphabet, women's suffrage and new laws. Turkey joins NATO and becomes a regional power bridging Europe and Asia.

sources.title: History of the Republic of Turkey
Proclamation of the Republic of Turkey

eras.title: The State of Israel
eras.text: Founded in 1948 amid war with its Arab neighbours. Further wars follow, and the conflict with the Palestinians over land and statehood remains unresolved.

eras.title: The Saudi states
eras.text: An alliance between the Al Saud and the reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab creates successive states in central Arabia; Ibn Saud conquers most of the peninsula in the early 20th century.

eras.title: The Kingdom
eras.text: Ibn Saud proclaims the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932. Oil, discovered in 1938, makes it one of the world's largest oil producers; the kingdom is the guardian of Mecca and Medina.
